extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in science, education, and literature (readers of Popular Science Monthly); teachers and college administrators for the self-government piece; language instructors for the German-method notice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for reviewing and describing books and educational/technical methods in a general-interest scientific and literary magazine; includes standards for textbook quality, author qualifications, pedagogical method descriptions, and reporting scientific apparatus/experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook suitability for general education
rubrics_metrics.description: A textbook should 'sum up the leading facts and fundamental principles of the science in an authoritative and trustworthy manner' and be presented 'in a form convenient and suitable for general use.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should be compact, well-organized, and authoritative; suitable for students in high schools and colleges and accessible to ordinary readers; cover major topics in due proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author qualifications for textbook authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Only 'a master who knows his subject at first hand, broadly and thoroughly, can be trusted' to prepare an authoritative textbook; not the work of an ordinary compiler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for prior original works, pioneer status in the field, and deep first-hand familiarity with subject-matter; the author's previous major studies support trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unifying theory/frame (example: evolution in anthropology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific study should be pursued 'in the light of the doctrine of evolution' which 'brings the facts ... into order, and gives organic method to the science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subject-treatment should adopt the appropriate unifying theoretical framework to order facts and give method; chapters/content should be organized around that conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive topical coverage in a textbook
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory manual should cover broad ground (e.g., man, races, language, writing, arts of life, arts of pleasure, science, religion, history, society) while keeping treatment full and satisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear table of contents or chapter-synopsis showing coverage of foundational topics; ensure each major domain is treated with sufficient depth for the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychology popular-science treatment (study of illusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work on illusions should view the subject 'in its relation to the process of just and accurate perception,' treating illusions as part of normal as well as pathological mental life and defining terms clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address both normal and pathological phenomena, provide a provisional definition (e.g., illusion as error counterfeiting the form of immediate/self-evident knowledge), give psychological analysis, and keep the exposition accessible rather than overly technical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and classification clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating a conceptual subject (e.g., illusions), the author should offer a clear provisional definition and explain distinctions (e.g., illusion vs fallacy; primary/intuitive vs secondary/inferential knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the definition as a working tool to organize subsequent chapters and to explain how types of phenomena relate and pass into one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary-style evaluation: primacy of style
rubrics_metrics.description: In literature, 'literary form is the main thing in the art of authorship' — style (the 'verbal dress') largely determines place and permanence of literary productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess an author's mastery of style, use of rhetorical devices (personification, apostrophe, hyperbole), pictorial illustration, and how these give force to familiar ideas; provide illustrative quotations and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authoritative examples and references in essays/reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: An essay or review should be supported by a 'formidable array of arguments, illustrations, and authorities' and be liberally referenced and quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite exemplary passages from influential authors to illustrate points, and aggregate respected authorities to strengthen evaluative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principles for a modern language course
rubrics_metrics.description: Course plan features: exclusive use of the target language without aid of the learner's vernacular; attention to grammatical and lexical details; deduction of rules from examples; teaching by contrast and association; graded lessons made up of conversations on familiar topics to supply vocabulary for daily use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lessons should be graded, conversational, and oriented to everyday vocabulary; rules should be induced from examples rather than given abstractly; emphasize speaking and comprehension in the target language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting scientific apparatus and experimental method
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing a new instrument (e.g., the Bolometer), acknowledge limitations of existing methods (e.g., prism misplacing heat-curve maximum), describe new apparatus construction and operation, and report unexpected scientific conclusions derived from its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe apparatus design and operation clearly; explain why it improves measurement; present experimental results and their implications (e.g., distribution of solar heat across spectrum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental rigor and duration in therapeutic/technical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Therapeutic claims (e.g., mechanical vibration as an anaesthetic) should be presented as the result of 'several years of experimenting' to determine appropriate apparatus forms and methods of application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report essential facts, describe apparatus forms (requirements such as due rapidity of motion and shortness of stroke), document varied methods tested for different pathological conditions, and publish findings in journals or book form for scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus design criteria for mechanical vibration therapy
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of apparatus required 'admit of considerable variety' provided only that 'due rapidity of motion and shortness of stroke' are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing therapeutic vibration devices, prioritize achieving sufficient vibration rate and short stroke; test variations to match different neural/pathological conditions and report progressive effects (e.g., increased anesthetic effect with increased vibration rate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological explanation requirement for therapeutic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Therapeutic efficacy should be linked to plausible physiological mechanisms (e.g., transmitted energy merging with vital system operations, increased oxidation, destruction of toxic retained waste, and 'functional revulsion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer a physiological account connecting the intervention to observed effects (temperature rise, improved capillary motion, removal of congestion) and provide observable intermediate effects as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational reform goal: cultivate self-government and character
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'essential and supreme work of education is to form character by the cultivation of self-control,' which implies liberty and responsibility and must be learned by practice rather than precept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education systems should create opportunities for students to exercise self-direction; self-government must be implemented as an exercised discipline (like music), not merely preached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model of college self-government via contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Place student and college on equal footing via a mutual voluntary engagement: 'Every student upon entering college signs an agreement to observe its laws' — the contract defines membership and consequences of breach (end of contract and membership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty act as helpers rather than police; intervention occurs only on contract breach; the college should still screen applicants (inquire into antecedents) and not admit indiscriminately; expelled students become visitors if they attend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected outcomes and advantages of student self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-government produces higher tone among students, freedom from being watched, reduced faculty policing, greater self-accountability, and improved deportment; it avoids antagonism between students and authorities and disciplines students in 'moral self-culture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating governance reforms, look for measurable changes in student conduct, tone, and reduced need for external coercive measures; consider self-government as preparation for responsibilities of practical life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of corporal punishment and external coercion in education
rubrics_metrics.description: External compulsion (symbolized by the rod) is adverse to forming self-control; the best teachers reject corporal punishment and its use indicates incapacity to govern by better methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess school governance by the degree to which coercive measures are replaced by voluntary, responsibility-based approaches; prefer milder methods and practices that cultivate intrinsic motivation.
